title: Alike and different: features we inherit and skills we learn

summary.text: Practice will not make your thumb longer. Practice will make your throwing better. That is the difference between a feature you inherit and a skill you learn. Features like eye colour and curly hair come from genes, tiny instructions you get from both parents. Skills like speaking Telugu or drawing a kolam come from practice and from the people around you, and a parent cannot pass them on at birth. Your child tests this with paper balls, a bucket and a strip of paper, then asks the family what they inherited and what they learned.
summary.art: A girl in a flat throwing a scrunched newspaper ball at a steel bucket with her left hand, while a strip of paper with a pencil mark lies beside her thumb on the floor.

intro.hook: Hold out your thumb. Can you make it longer by practising? Now think of throwing a ball. Can you get better at that by practising?
intro.text: Some things about you came from your parents before you were born. Other things you learned after you were born. They feel the same, because they are all part of you. In this unit you find out which is which. You test it with a bucket, a few paper balls and a strip of paper. Then you ask your family what they inherited, what they learned, and who taught them.
intro.art: A child holding up one thumb next to a strip of paper, with a bucket and three paper balls on the floor behind.

outcomes: By the end I can say what it means to inherit a feature, and name some features I inherited.
By the end I can name skills I learned, and say who or what helped me learn them.
By the end I can test whether practice changes a skill or a body feature, and say what I found.
By the end I can say why a skill a parent learned is not passed on to their baby at birth.
By the end I can give an example of something that comes from both genes and life, like height.
By the end I can say that other animals and plants learn too, and give an example.

terms.meaning: To inherit a feature is to get it from your parents, through their genes. It starts before you are born.
terms.example: Revathi inherited her curly hair from her family.
terms.art: A mother and a daughter side by side, both with the same curly hair.

terms.meaning: A characteristic is a feature of how a being looks or what they are like. It is another word for feature.
terms.example: Brown eyes, a dimple and long fingers are characteristics.
terms.art: A child's face with arrows pointing to the eyes, a dimple and the ears.

terms.meaning: A gene is a tiny instruction inside the cells of a living being. Genes help build the body. You get half of yours from your mother and half from your father.
terms.example: Genes help decide the colour of your eyes.
terms.art: A simple picture of a child, with a zoom-in circle showing a tiny twisted thread inside one cell.

terms.meaning: To learn is to come to know something, or to be able to do something, by trying, watching or being taught.
terms.example: Farhana learned Tamil from her friends at school.
terms.art: Two girls talking and laughing at a school gate.

terms.meaning: A skill is something you can do well because you have practised it.
terms.example: Riding a cycle, swimming and drawing a kolam are skills.
terms.art: A girl riding a cycle in a building compound, with her sister running behind.

terms.meaning: To practise is to do something again and again, so that you get better at it.
terms.example: Meera practised her kolam every morning for a week.
terms.art: A row of seven small kolam drawings on paper, the first wobbly and the last neat.

explanations.definition: An inherited feature is one that comes from the genes you got from your parents.
explanations.description: Inside the cells of your body are tiny instructions called genes. You got half of them from your mother and half from your father. Genes help decide many features: the colour of your eyes, whether your hair is curly, the shape of your ears. Some inherited features show at birth. Others grow later, like your adult teeth. Practice does not change them. In the Practice Test, your thumb stayed the same length, however much you wiggled it.
examples: Brown eyes like a parent's, or a dimple like a grandparent's, come from genes.
Curly hair can be straightened for a day. The new hair still grows out curly.
A kitten inherits the colour of her fur from her parents.
explanations.context: This card is about features that come from your parents, through genes.
explanations.art: A girl looking into a mirror, with small pictures of her mother's dimple and her father's eyes beside her reflection.

explanations.definition: A learned skill is something you can do because you practised it, or because someone showed you how.
explanations.description: Nobody is born riding a cycle, speaking Telugu or drawing a kolam. You learn these by watching, trying, and trying again. Each try changes you a little, and the connections between the cells in your brain change too. Eleanor Maguire, a scientist in London, found that taxi drivers who had learned thousands of streets had a bigger part of the brain that helps with finding the way. In the Practice Test, your throws got better in just five minutes.
examples: A girl in Pune learns to ride a cycle while her sister holds the seat.
A boy in Kochi learns to swim in a pool with a teacher.
A child in Guwahati learns a Bihu song by singing along with her aunt.
explanations.context: This card is about skills: things you can do because you practised them.
explanations.art: Three small scenes: a girl on a cycle with her sister holding the seat, a boy swimming with a teacher, a girl singing with her aunt.

explanations.concept: Many things are a bit of both
explanations.definition: Many features come from genes and also from the life a being lives.
explanations.description: Height is a good example. Genes from both parents set about how tall a child can grow. Good food, sleep and health help the child reach that height. Language is another example. Every baby is born able to learn any language. Janet Werker, a scientist in Canada, found that babies of 6 to 8 months can hear the difference between sounds that are used in Hindi, Tamil and Telugu. By 10 to 12 months, babies from English-speaking homes mostly cannot. Their ears have tuned in to the language around them.
examples: Two bean plants from the same packet grow to different heights if one sits in the sun and one in a dark corner.
A child with tall parents grows taller with good food than with too little food.
A baby born in Chennai to Bengali-speaking parents can grow up speaking both Bengali and Tamil.
explanations.context: This card is about features that come partly from genes and partly from how a being lives.
explanations.art: A wall chart of a child's height, with pencil marks at different ages, beside a plate of idli, sambar and a banana.

explanations.concept: A skill is not passed on at birth
explanations.definition: What a parent learns or does to their body during their life does not pass to their baby at birth.
explanations.description: A mother who is a great singer has a baby who must still learn to sing. A father who lifts heavy sacks builds strong arms. His baby is not born with those strong arms. Long ago, many people thought such changes were passed on, but tests showed it was not true. Skills pass from person to person by teaching and copying, so a skill can go to anyone who learns it.
examples: A baby adopted into a Malayalam-speaking home grows up speaking Malayalam, whatever language the birth parents spoke.
A Bharatanatyam dancer's daughter learns to dance in classes, step by step, like every other student.
A grandmother who draws kolams can teach her granddaughter, and also the girl next door.
explanations.context: This card says why a parent's skills do not come to a baby at birth, and how skills travel instead.
explanations.art: A grandmother teaching two girls to draw a kolam on a doorstep, one girl her granddaughter and one a neighbour in a school uniform.

explanations.concept: Other animals, and plants, learn too
explanations.description: Humans are one kind of animal, and other animals learn as well. A young male zebra finch learns his song by listening to an older male. A young finch who never hears another finch sings a strange, broken song. Young chimpanzees learn to fish for termites with a stick by watching their mothers. Some scientists say plants learn too. Monica Gagliano dropped touch-me-not plants gently, again and again, and after many harmless drops they stopped folding their leaves. Other scientists call this habituation, a simple kind of getting used to something, and want more tests.
examples: A kitten gets better at hunting by watching her mother and playing with her sisters and brothers.
A young zebra finch sings his father's kind of song.
A touch-me-not plant learns that a gentle drop is harmless.

perspectives.who: Monica Gagliano and other plant scientists
perspectives.explanation: The touch-me-not plants changed what they did after many harmless drops, and kept the change for weeks. They still folded when shaken, so they had not just got tired. That is learning and remembering.
They call it habituation, a simple kind of getting used to something. They want more tests before they call it learning in the way a finch learns a song.

explanations.context: This card is about learning in other animals and in plants.
explanations.art: A zebra finch father singing on a perch with a young finch listening beside him, and a touch-me-not plant with open leaves in a pot below.

agreed.text: Many features, like eye colour and hair shape, come from genes we get from both parents.
agreed.evidence: Scientists can read a person's genes and match them to features. Features like these follow clear patterns in families.
agreed.context: This card is about what scientists agree on: many features come from genes.

agreed.text: Skills a parent learns are not passed on to their baby at birth.
agreed.evidence: Babies adopted into a family grow up speaking the language of that family, not the language of their birth parents. Scientists have tested many times whether changes to a parent's body pass to babies, and they do not.
agreed.context: This card is about what scientists agree on: skills have to be learned again by each child.

agreed.text: Practice changes the body, and also the brain.
agreed.evidence: Eleanor Maguire found that London taxi drivers who learned thousands of streets had a bigger part of the brain that helps with finding the way. Muscles grow stronger with use.
agreed.context: This card is about what scientists agree on: practice changes the one who practises.

challenging.claim: Some people are born with a talent, and practice does not matter much.
challenging.for: Studies of twins show that genes do shape how quickly a person learns some skills, like music or running.
challenging.against: Nobody is born playing the veena or drawing a kolam. Even people with a gift for a skill practise for years to become good at it.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that talent is born, not made.

challenging.claim: Changes a parent makes to their own body are passed on to their children.
challenging.who: Many people, including Jean-Baptiste Lamarck in 1809
challenging.for: Children of strong, hard-working parents are often strong, and children of musicians are often musical.
challenging.against: Tests found that changes to a parent's body, such as muscles built by hard work, are not passed on. Children of musicians usually grow up hearing music every day, so they learn it at home.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea: that what parents do to their bodies passes to their babies.

challenging.claim: Being left-handed is a bad habit, so children should be made to write with the right hand.
challenging.who: A common idea in many places, including India, until not long ago
challenging.for: Most tools and desks are made for right-handed people, so life can be easier for them.
challenging.against: About 1 person in 10 is left-handed. It runs partly in families and starts before birth. It is not a habit. Forcing a child to switch hands makes writing harder for them.
challenging.context: This card is about left-handedness, and the old idea that it should be trained out.

big_questions.q: If an older person teaches you a song, and one day you teach it to your own child, whose song is it?
big_questions.hint: Think about where the song lives. Is it in the person who taught you, in you, or in everyone who sings it?

big_questions.q: Is a language something a family owns, or something anyone can learn?
big_questions.hint: Think about a child from another state who learned your language at school.

big_questions.q: Two children practise the same amount. Must they become equally good?
big_questions.hint: Think about the idea that genes can help some people learn a skill faster. Does that mean practice does not matter?

big_questions.q: A baby can hear the sounds of every language. Most grown-ups cannot. What happens in between?
big_questions.hint: Remember Janet Werker's babies, and the two 't' sounds.

story.title: Paati's Kolam Hands
story.note: Meera, Paati, Arun, Farhana and their families are made up. It is true that a skill like drawing a kolam is learned by practice, and that a child learns the language spoken around them.
text: Meera was seven. She lived on the fourth floor of a block of flats in Chennai. Every morning, her Paati drew a kolam on the floor outside their door.
Paati made a grid of dots with rice flour. Then she let the flour fall from her fingers in thin white lines, looping round and round the dots. The lines never wobbled.
Meera's cousin Arun was staying with them for the holidays. He watched Paati and said, 'Meera will draw kolams like that too. It runs in the family. She was born with Paati's hands.'
Meera liked the sound of that. She held up her hands next to Paati's. 'Look, Paati. My fingers are long and thin, like yours.'
'They are,' said Paati, smiling. 'You got those fingers from our family. Your Amma has them too.'

The next morning, Meera woke up early. She took a pinch of rice flour, the way Paati did, and made five dots in a row. She tried to loop a line round them. The flour came out in a lump. The line went crooked, and then it broke.
Meera's eyes filled with tears. 'Arun was wrong,' she said. 'I did not get Paati's kolam hands.'

Paati sat down on the step beside her. 'Do you know what my first kolam looked like?' she asked. 'I was your age, in a village near Thanjavur. My lines were all bumps and gaps. My mother laughed so hard that she had to sit down.'
'But yours are perfect now,' said Meera.

'I have drawn a kolam almost every morning for sixty years,' said Paati. 'My fingers learned it, one morning at a time. You got my long fingers when you were born. The kolam is something you have to learn.'

Just then, their neighbour Farhana came out of the next flat with her school bag. Her family had moved from Kolkata last year. 'Vanakkam, Paati!' she called. Then she said something in quick Tamil that made Paati laugh.

'Farhana's Ammi and Abbu speak Bengali at home,' Paati told Meera. 'A year ago, Farhana knew no Tamil at all. Now she chats in Tamil with her friends every day. Nobody is born with a language. Every child learns the words that people say around them.'
Meera thought about that. 'So I got my long fingers from you,' she said slowly. 'But I can only get your kolam if you teach me.'
'Yes,' said Paati. 'And I can teach anyone who wants to learn. Farhana too.'

So every morning that week, Meera drew a kolam on a sheet of paper first, and then on the floor. Farhana joined her on two mornings. Paati showed them how to hold the flour between the thumb and the first finger, and how to move the hand slowly and evenly.

On Monday, Meera's line broke four times. On Wednesday, it broke twice. On Saturday, her five-dot kolam went all the way round without a single break. The loops were not as round as Paati's. But they were her own.
Meera laid all her paper kolams out in a row on the floor. Arun came to look. 'See?' he said. 'I told you. It runs in the family.'

Meera shook her head. 'My fingers run in the family,' she said. 'My kolam came from practice. Look, you can see it getting better every day.' She pointed to Farhana's kolam. 'Farhana's got better too, and she is not in our family.'
Arun looked at the row of kolams for a long time. Then he picked up the rice flour. 'Can you teach me?' he asked.
Meera grinned and gave him the flour. 'Start with five dots,' she said.
story.epiphany: Meera sees that she inherited Paati's long fingers, but not Paati's kolam. The kolam is a skill that comes from practice and teaching, so anyone can learn it, even someone outside the family.
ask: What did Meera get from her family when she was born?
Why was Meera's first kolam crooked, when Paati's lines never wobble?
Arun said the kolam runs in the family. What did Meera show him?
art: A grandmother in a cotton sari drawing a looping white kolam on the floor outside a flat door, with a girl and a boy watching.
A girl crouching at a doorstep, looking sadly at a broken, crooked line of rice flour round five dots.
A girl in a school uniform with a school bag waving from the next flat door, while the grandmother laughs.
Seven paper kolams laid out in a row on a floor, getting neater from left to right, with three children looking at them.

games.title: Born, Learned or Both? A sorting game
games.context: In this game you sort cards into three piles: things we are born with, things we learn, and things that come from a bit of both. Each card has the answer on the back.

items.b: Born with it. Eye colour comes from the genes you got from your parents.
Learned it. A baby learns the language spoken around them.
Learned it. Everyone wobbles at first, and gets better with practice.
Born with it. Curly hair comes from genes. Straightened hair still grows out curly.
Learned it. It takes many mornings of practice.
Both. Genes set about how tall you can grow. Good food and health help you get there.
Learned it. People learn to swim with practice, often with a teacher.
Born with it. A dimple comes from the genes you got from your parents.
Learned it. Someone shows you, and you try it many times.

items.f: A newborn baby holding a finger tightly
items.b: Born with it. Babies can grip a finger tightly from the day they are born.

items.f: A duckling swimming the day after she hatches
items.b: Born with it. Ducklings can swim almost as soon as they hatch.

items.f: A young zebra finch singing his song
items.b: Learned it. He learns the song by listening to an older male finch.
Both. It runs partly in families. But even identical twins can use different hands.
Born with it. Ear shape comes from genes.
Learned it. Children in Assam learn Bihu songs from the people around them.
Both. Genes help shape your legs and muscles. Training makes you faster.

printables.title: 3 sorting mats, one on each sheet
items: Born with it
Learned it
Both

rules: Lay the three mats on the floor: Born with it, Learned it, and Both.
Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, words up.
Take turns. On your turn, take the top card. Read it, or ask a grown-up to read it.
Say which mat it goes on, and why. Then turn the card over to check the answer.
If you were right, you score 1 point. If you were wrong, you score nothing. Either way, put the card on the right mat.
Play until all 16 cards are on the mats. The player with the most points wins. If you tie, you all win. If you play alone, try to beat your own score next time.

setup.art: Three sheets of paper on a floor, labelled Born with it, Learned it, and Both, with a pile of small cards beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the three mats and the pile of cards.

setup.art: A child placing a card that says Riding a cycle on the Learned it mat, while a grown-up holds the next card.
setup.caption: 2. Put each card on a mat, then turn it over to check.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 16 cards. 2. Lay the three mats on the floor. 3. Read the rules aloud.
flow.say: Some things about us come from our parents' genes. Some we learn. Some are a bit of both. Let us sort these cards and see.
flow.kid: Look at the three mats. Born with it. Learned it. Both.

flow.do: 1. Take turns with the cards. 2. Ask for a reason each time. 3. Turn the card over to check. 4. Give 1 point for a right answer.
flow.say: Speaking Telugu. Which mat? Why do you think so? Now turn it over and check.
flow.kid: Read the card. Pick a mat. Say why. Turn it over.

ask.q: Why does riding a cycle go on Learned it?
good: Nobody is born riding a cycle.
You have to practise to get better.

flow.parent: Accept any good reason, then let the back of the card decide. The Both cards are the tricky ones. Talk about them a little longer.

flow.do: Count the cards on each mat together and add up the points, then ask the last question.
flow.say: Which mat has the most cards? Which player has the most points? Was any card a surprise?
flow.kid: Count the cards on each mat. Count your points. Which card surprised you?

check.q: Which card goes on the Both mat?
check.why: Height comes from genes and from good food and health. Eye colour comes from genes. Making rasam is learned.

games.title: How Did They Learn? A memory game
games.context: This is a memory game with 8 pairs of cards. One card in each pair shows someone with a skill. The other card says how that skill was learned.

printables.title: 16 memory cards to cut out, in 8 pairs
items: A girl in Kochi speaks Malayalam.
The girl in Kochi heard her family speak Malayalam every day.
A young chimpanzee fishes for termites with a stick.
The young chimpanzee watched her mother fish with a stick, many times.
A young zebra finch sings his song.
The young zebra finch listened to an older male finch sing.
A boy in Pune rides a cycle.
The boy in Pune practised while his sister held the seat.
A girl in Madurai draws a kolam.
The girl in Madurai was shown by her Paati, morning after morning.
A touch-me-not plant stays open when dropped gently.
The touch-me-not plant was dropped gently many times, and was never hurt.
A kitten catches a paper ball.
The kitten watched her mother hunt, and played with her sisters and brothers.
A girl in Imphal plays football well.
The girl in Imphal played football with her friends every evening.

rules: Mix the 16 cards and lay them face down in 4 rows of 4.
On your turn, turn over two cards and read them aloud.
If the two cards belong together, one showing a skill and one saying how that same skill was learned, you keep the pair and have another turn.
If not, turn them face down again. The next player has a turn.
When all 8 pairs are found, the player with the most pairs wins. If you tie, you all win.

setup.art: Sixteen small cards face down on a floor mat in four rows of four, with two children kneeling beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the cards face down in 4 rows of 4.

setup.art: A child turning over two cards, one showing a girl drawing a kolam and one showing a grandmother teaching.
setup.caption: 2. Turn over two cards. Does the skill match how it was learned?

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 16 cards. 2. Mix them and lay them face down in 4 rows of 4.
flow.say: Each skill card has a partner card that says how the skill was learned. Let us find the pairs.
flow.kid: Lay the cards face down. Find a skill and how it was learned.

flow.do: Take turns turning over two cards. Read both aloud each time.
flow.say: A boy in Pune rides a cycle. The boy in Pune practised while his sister held the seat. Do those two belong together?
flow.kid: Turn over two cards. Read them. Do they belong together?

ask.q: Who taught the young zebra finch his song?

flow.parent: The touch-me-not card may surprise your child. Scientists dropped these plants gently many times, and the plants stopped folding their leaves. Some scientists say this is learning, and some say it is getting used to something.

flow.do: When all pairs are found, ask the last question.
flow.say: Now think about all eight skills. Which of them did someone have from the day they were born?
flow.kid: Which of these skills were there from birth?

ask.q: Were any of these skills there from birth?
good: They all needed someone to watch, or lots of tries.

experiments.title: The Practice Test: what can practice change?
experiments.context: In this experiment you practise two things for five minutes. One is throwing paper balls into a bucket. The other is wiggling and stretching your thumb. You measure both before and after, to see what practice changes.
experiments.question: If you practise throwing for five minutes, will more balls land in the bucket? If you practise stretching your thumb, will your thumb get longer?
experiments.predict: Guess first. After five minutes of practice, will more balls go in the bucket? Will your thumb be longer? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We throw from the same line, at the same bucket, with the same three balls, every round. We count 10 throws in each round, because one throw can be lucky. We measure the thumb with the same strip of paper each time, in the same way.
results_table: Balls in the bucket, out of 10

materials.item: 3 balls made from newspaper, each one sheet scrunched up tightly, or 3 pairs of rolled-up socks
a bucket, a big steel vessel or a laundry basket
a strip of paper about 2 cm wide and as long as your hand, and a pencil
a chappal or a piece of tape to mark the throwing line
a phone timer or a clock

schedule.what: Guess. Measure the thumb. Throw 10. Practise for five minutes. Throw 10 again. Measure the thumb again. Compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for Round 1 and Round 2. Stick the thumb strip under the table.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
cols: Balls in the bucket, out of 10

setup.art: A strip of paper laid along a child's thumb from the tip to the crease at the base, with a pencil making a small mark.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the strip along your thumb. Mark where your thumb ends.

setup.art: A child standing behind a chappal on the floor, throwing a scrunched newspaper ball at a bucket two big steps away, using the hand she does not write with.
setup.caption: 2. Stand at the line. Throw 10 balls with the hand you do not write with.

setup.art: A child throwing again and again at the bucket while a phone timer shows five minutes.
setup.caption: 3. Practise for five minutes. Then throw 10 again and measure your thumb again.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the bucket, the balls and the paper strip. 2. Ask both questions, and for a reason each time. 3. Write the guesses at the top of a sheet for your child.
flow.say: We are going to practise two things. Throwing, and stretching your thumb. After five minutes, will more balls go in? Will your thumb be longer? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: You will practise throwing. You will practise stretching your thumb. Guess what will change. Why?

ask.q: Will your thumb be longer after practice?
good: No, because a thumb does not grow from practice.
Maybe a tiny bit, if I stretch it hard.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine. Write it down and say nothing yet. Some children think stretching might make the thumb longer. The test will show them.

flow.do: 1. Your child uses the hand they do not write with. They lay the strip along that thumb, with the end of the strip level with the tip of the thumb. 2. You make a small pencil mark on the strip at the crease where the thumb joins the hand. 3. Write 'before' next to the mark.
flow.say: Lay the strip along your thumb, from the tip to the line where your thumb joins your hand. Hold still while I mark it.
flow.kid: Lay the strip on your thumb. Hold still. We mark where it ends.
flow.parent: Always measure from the same place, the tip of the thumb to the crease at the base. That keeps the test fair.

flow.do: 1. Put the bucket two big steps away from the chappal line. 2. Your child throws 10 times with the hand they do not write with. 3. Count the balls that land in and stay in. 4. Pick up the balls after every three throws. 5. Write the number in the table as Round 1.
flow.say: Stand behind the line. Use the hand you do not write with. Throw 10 times. I will count how many go in.
flow.kid: Stand at the line. Use your other hand. Throw 10 times. Count with me.
flow.parent: We use the hand your child does not write with, so there is lots of room to get better.

flow.do: 1. Set a timer for five minutes. 2. Your child keeps throwing from the same line, with the same hand, and picks up the balls when they are all thrown. 3. Every minute, your child also wiggles and stretches the thumb 10 times.
flow.say: Now practise. Watch where each ball lands, and change your throw a little each time. Every minute, stretch your thumb 10 times too.
flow.kid: Practise throwing for five minutes. Watch where the ball lands. Stretch your thumb too.

ask.q: What are you changing as you practise?

flow.do: 1. Your child throws 10 more times from the same line. 2. Count the balls that land in and write it as Round 2. 3. Measure the thumb again with the same strip, and mark it 'after'.
flow.say: Now the real test again. Ten throws. Then let us measure your thumb with the same strip.
flow.kid: Throw 10 times again. Count. Then measure your thumb again.

check.q: What did you find after practice?
options: More balls went in, and the thumb stayed the same
check.why: Practice changes a skill, like throwing. It does not change a body feature, like the length of your thumb, which grew from genes.

flow.parent: If the number did not go up, that can happen in one short session. Practise again tomorrow for five minutes and test again. Scores usually rise with more practice. The new thumb mark should be in the same place, or within the width of a pencil line. A tiny difference comes from measuring, not from growing.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child three things, one at a time. What did you find? What did you see that shows it? Why do you think it happened? 2. Then read the explanation cards together.
flow.say: So, what changed with practice? What did you see that tells you? Why do you think the throws changed, but the thumb did not?
flow.kid: Say what you found. Say what you saw. Why do you think it happened?
flow.parent: A strong answer: more balls went in after practice, but the thumb mark stayed in the same place. Throwing is a skill, so practice changes it. The length of the thumb is a feature inherited through genes, so practice does not change it. Let your child say it in their own words first.

activities.title: Born With It or Learned It? A family survey
activities.context: In this activity you ask two or three people in your family about themselves. You find one feature each person inherited, and one skill each person learned, and who taught them.

materials.item: a sheet of paper with a table drawn on it, and a pencil
two or three family members, at home or on a phone call

schedule.what: Ask family members what they inherited and what they learned. Fill in the table.

activities.record: A table with four columns: Person, A feature they inherited, A skill they learned, Who taught them.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a hand-drawn table of four columns: Person, Inherited, Learned, Who taught them.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the table with four columns (a grown-up can help).

setup.art: A girl holding a phone to talk with her grandmother on a video call, with the table and a pencil in front of her.
setup.caption: 2. Ask each person your questions and fill in a row.

flow.do: 1. Draw a table with four columns: Person, A feature they inherited, A skill they learned, Who taught them. 2. Choose two or three people to ask.
flow.say: We are going to be scientists who ask questions. For each person, we find one thing they got from their parents, and one thing they learned.
flow.kid: Draw the table. Choose two or three people to ask.

flow.do: Your child asks each person these questions, and you help write the answers in the table. 1. What is one feature you got from your parents? 2. What is one thing you learned to do? 3. Who taught you?
flow.say: Ask each person: what feature did you get from your parents? What is one thing you learned to do? Who taught you?
flow.kid: Ask each person. What did you get from your parents? What did you learn? Who taught you?
flow.parent: Families are made in many ways. If your child is adopted, or some relatives are far away, ask anyone in the household. The learned column works for everyone.

flow.do: Look at the table together and ask the questions below.
flow.say: Look at the Who taught them column. Was it always a parent? Did anyone learn something from a friend, a teacher or a neighbour?
flow.kid: Look at the table. Who taught each skill? Was it always a parent?

ask.q: Did every skill come from a parent?
good: No, one person learned to cycle from a brother.
No, one person learned English at school.

activities.title: What Could I Do When I Was Born?
activities.context: In this activity you ask a grown-up what you could do on the day you were born, and what you learned later. You make a two-column chart.

materials.item: a sheet of paper and crayons
baby photos or videos on a phone, if you have them

schedule.what: Ask a grown-up about the day you were born. Make a chart of born-able and learned-later.

activities.record: A chart with two columns: Born able to, and Learned later. Draw one picture in each column.

setup.art: A mother showing her child a baby photo on a phone, the baby holding an adult's finger tightly.
setup.caption: 1. Look at baby photos and ask what you could do.

setup.art: A sheet with two columns, Born able to and Learned later, with drawings of a crying baby and a child riding a cycle.
setup.caption: 2. Make a chart with two columns.

flow.do: 1. Show your child a baby photo or video, if you have one. 2. Tell them what they could do as a newborn: cry, drink milk, sneeze, grip a finger tightly.
flow.say: On the day you were born, you could already cry, drink milk and hold my finger very tightly. Nobody taught you those.
flow.kid: Look at you as a baby! You could cry and hold a finger tight.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to name things they learned later. Walking, talking, eating with their fingers, using the toilet, writing their name. 2. Your child draws one thing in each column.
flow.say: What can you do now that you could not do as a baby? Who helped you learn it?
flow.kid: What can you do now? Who helped you learn? Draw it.

ask.q: What did you learn after you were born?

flow.do: Ask the last question and let your child think.
flow.say: Your list of things you learned is much longer than your list of things you were born able to do. Why do you think that is?
flow.kid: Which list is longer? Why?
flow.parent: There is no single answer. Human babies are born able to do only a few things, and learn most things later from the people around them.

activities.title: Three New Words
activities.context: In this activity you learn three words in a language you do not speak yet, from someone who does. The next day you check if you still remember them.

materials.item: a family member, neighbour or friend who speaks another language, at home or on a phone call

schedule.what: Learn three words from someone who speaks another language.
Say the three words again without help.

activities.record: You write the three words and what they mean (or your child draws them). Put a tick by each one your child remembered the next day.

setup.art: A girl sitting with an older woman neighbour who is teaching her words, both smiling, with a notebook between them.
setup.caption: 1. Ask someone to teach you three words.

setup.art: A child saying words aloud the next morning, with a notebook showing three words and ticks beside them.
setup.caption: 2. The next day, say them without help.

flow.do: 1. Find someone who speaks a language your child does not. A grandparent's language, a neighbour's, a friend's, or a relative on a phone call. 2. Your child asks them for three words: water, thank you, and good morning. 3. Your child says each word five times. 4. You write each word down, with what it means.
flow.say: Ask them how to say water, thank you and good morning in their language. Say each word five times.
flow.kid: Ask for three words. Water. Thank you. Good morning. Say each one five times.
flow.parent: Any language works: Konkani, Tulu, Bengali, Mizo, Urdu, Kannada, or a language from abroad. The point is that your child was not born with these words, and learns them now.

flow.do: The next day, your child says the three words without help. Tick the ones they remember.
flow.say: Can you still say the three words? You were not born knowing them. Now they are part of you.
flow.kid: Say your three words. Did you remember them?

ask.q: Where did these words come from?
good: I learned them from the person who taught me.

flow.parent: It is fine if your child forgot one word. That shows how practice keeps a skill. Say the word again together a few times.

projects.title: Seven-Day Kolam: watch a skill grow
projects.context: In this project you draw the same small kolam on paper every day for seven days. You keep every drawing, and count how many times your line breaks. Then you lay them in a row to see the skill grow.

materials.item: 7 sheets of paper, or a notebook
a pencil, or white chalk on black paper

schedule.what: Draw five dots and loop one line round them. Count the breaks in your line. Write the date.
Draw the same kolam. Count the breaks.
Draw the same kolam. Count the breaks.
Draw the same kolam. Count the breaks.
Draw the same kolam. Count the breaks.
Draw the same kolam. Count the breaks.
Draw the kolam one last time. Lay all seven in a row and compare.

projects.record: Seven kolam drawings with the date and the number of breaks on each. A row of numbers from day 1 to day 7.

setup.art: Five pencil dots in a row on white paper, with one looping line going round them like a chain.
setup.caption: 1. Make five dots. Loop one line round them without lifting the pencil.

setup.art: Seven small kolam drawings laid in a row on a floor, the first crooked with gaps and the last smooth and neat.
setup.caption: 2. On day 7, lay all seven drawings in a row.

flow.do: 1. Draw the pattern for your child to copy: five dots in a row, about two finger-widths apart. 2. Your child draws their own five dots. 3. Your child loops one line round all the dots, over and under the row, back to the start. 4. The pencil must not lift. 5. Count the places where the line broke or the pencil lifted. 6. Write the date and the number.
flow.say: Every day this week, you will draw this same kolam. Today is day 1. Let us count how many times your line breaks.
flow.kid: Make five dots. Loop one line round them. Count the breaks.
flow.parent: Use the same pattern every day, so you can compare fairly. A break is any place where the line stops and starts again.

flow.do: On days 2 to 6, your child draws the same kolam once. Count the breaks and write them down.
flow.say: Day 3. Same kolam. Go slowly and evenly. How many breaks today?
flow.kid: Draw the same kolam. Count the breaks. Write the number.
flow.wait: Come back every day until day 7.

flow.do: 1. On day 7, your child draws the kolam one last time. 2. Lay all seven drawings in a row. 3. Read the numbers of breaks aloud, from day 1 to day 7.
flow.say: Look at day 1 and day 7 side by side. What changed? Did your fingers change, or did your skill change?
flow.kid: Lay out all seven. Look at day 1 and day 7. What changed?

check.q: Your kolam got better over seven days. Why?
options: A kolam comes with your genes
check.why: Drawing a kolam is a skill. It gets better with practice. Your fingers stayed the same, and a skill does not come with genes.

challenges.title: Teach It in Five Minutes
challenges.context: This is a teaching challenge. Pick a small skill you can do and a grown-up does not know. Design the best way to teach it to them in five minutes.
challenges.problem: Teach a grown-up a small skill they do not know yet, in five minutes, so that at the end they can do it alone.
constraints: You may not do it for them.
At the end, they must do it alone, while you watch.
materials: a sheet of paper for a paper boat, or nothing at all for a clapping game
general: Show the whole skill slowly, once, before they try.
Break it into small steps, and teach one step at a time.
Let them try each step, and help only when they are stuck.
creative: Draw a picture guide with one step in each box.
Make up a short rhyme that says the steps in order.
Teach the whole skill without talking, only by showing.
challenges.your_turn: Now pick a new skill, and teach it to someone younger than you. Which way of teaching worked best?

setup.art: A girl showing her father how to fold a paper boat, holding a half-folded sheet slowly so he can see.
setup.caption: 1. Show the skill slowly, one step at a time.

setup.art: A father folding a paper boat on his own while his daughter watches, with a phone timer beside them.
setup.caption: 2. At the end, the grown-up does it alone.

flow.do: 1. Your child picks a skill: a paper boat, a clapping game, a three-dot kolam or a few words in another language. 2. Your child picks a grown-up who does not know it yet.
flow.say: You are the teacher today. Which skill will you teach, and to whom?
flow.kid: Pick a skill you can do. Pick a grown-up to teach.

flow.do: 1. Start the timer for five minutes. 2. Your child teaches. 3. The grown-up tries each step, and does not pretend to know it. 4. Use the rest of the time to set up and put things away.
flow.say: Teach me. I will try every step. If I get stuck, show me again.
flow.kid: Teach your grown-up. Show slowly. Let them try.
flow.parent: Be a real learner. Make the mistakes a beginner makes. This lets your child see how a skill passes from one person to another.

flow.do: The grown-up does the skill alone while your child watches. Then talk about it.
flow.say: I can do it now. I was not born knowing it. Where did my new skill come from?
flow.kid: Watch your grown-up do it alone. Where did their skill come from?

ask.q: Where did the grown-up's new skill come from?

items.p: Sort these into two groups: Born with it, and Learned it.
items: curly hair
Born with it
speaking Kannada
Learned it
brown eyes
Born with it
tying shoelaces
Learned it
the shape of your nose
Born with it
swimming
Learned it
items.why: Hair shape, eye colour and nose shape come from genes. Speaking a language, tying laces and swimming are learned by practice.
items.art: Six small pictures: curly hair, a girl talking, brown eyes, hands tying laces, a nose, a child swimming.

items.p: Draw your thumb strip from the Practice Test. Show the 'before' mark and the 'after' mark where they really were.
items.a: One strip with the two marks at the same place.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the two marks in the same place, because practice did not change the length of the thumb.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down. In the Practice Test, why did we throw 10 balls in each round, and not just 1?
items.a: One throw can be lucky or unlucky. Ten throws show how good you really are.
items.why: A strong answer says that one throw could be a fluke, so many throws make the test fair.

items.p: If you straighten curly hair for a day, the new hair that grows out will be straight.
items.why: False. Straightening changes only the hair you already have. The new hair grows from the same genes, so it comes out curly.

items.p: Draw a line from each skill to how it was learned.
pairs: Practising while someone held the seat
Hearing people speak it every day
Being shown, and trying every morning
Listening to an older male finch
items.why: Every one of these skills was learned, by practice, by listening or by being shown.

items.p: Mala, a girl in Class 2, and her brother Rohan listen to their aunt sing Carnatic music.

views.says: Our aunt sings so well because she practised for years.
Our aunt was born a singer. It is in her genes.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Say why. Then say one thing the other child might be right about.
items.a: Mala is closer. Nobody is born singing Carnatic music, so the aunt practised a lot. Rohan may be a little right: genes can help a voice, but they do not teach a song.
items.why: A strong answer says singing is learned by practice, and is fair to Rohan's idea that genes can help.

items.p: Here is Lakshmi, a girl in Class 2. Draw a ring round two things she inherited. Draw a box round two things she learned.
items.a: Rings round her curly hair and her dimple. Boxes round the veena she is playing and the Tamil book she is reading.
items.why: Hair shape and a dimple come from genes. Playing the veena and reading are skills she learned.
items.art: A girl with curly hair and a dimple, playing a veena, with a Tamil storybook open beside her.

items.p: Kamala, a girl in Class 2, asked 5 relatives who taught them a skill. 3 said a parent. The others said a teacher or a friend. How many did not learn from a parent?
items.why: 5 take away 3 leaves 2. So 2 people learned from someone who was not a parent.

items.p: To get better at a skill, you need to ________.
items.why: A skill gets better each time you practise it.

items.p: The shape of your hair comes from your ________.
items.why: Hair shape is an inherited feature. It comes from the genes you got from your parents.

items.p: Put these steps of learning to ride a cycle in order, from first to last.
items: You ride all the way down the road alone
Someone holds the seat while you pedal
You ride a little way alone
You wobble and put your feet down
a: Someone holds the seat while you pedal
You wobble and put your feet down
You ride a little way alone
You ride all the way down the road alone
items.why: A skill grows step by step. Each try makes you a little better.
items.art: Four small pictures in a mixed order: a child riding alone down a road, a sister holding a cycle seat, a child riding a short way, a child wobbling with feet down.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down. Priya, a girl in Class 2, has an Amma who is a wonderful cook. Was Priya born able to make rasam? What will she need to do?
items.a: No. Priya will need someone to show her, and she will need to practise many times.
items.why: A strong answer says cooking is a skill, so Priya must learn it. Her Amma can teach her.

items.p: Very young babies can hear the difference between the sounds of every language. What happens by the time they are one year old?
opts: They get better at the sounds of the language around them, and lose some others
They can hear no sounds at all
items.why: Janet Werker found that babies of 6 to 8 months could tell two Hindi 't' sounds apart, and by 10 to 12 months most could not. Their ears tune in to the language they hear.

items.p: Deepa and Grace, two girls in Mumbai, are talking about Deepa's uncle. He lifts heavy sacks at the market every day, and his arms are very strong. He and his wife are expecting a baby.

views.says: The baby will be born with strong arms, because the baby's father has strong arms.
The baby will get his genes, but not the muscles he built by lifting.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? What test could show who is right?
items.a: Grace is right. Muscles built by work are not passed on at birth. Deepa is right that strong parents often have strong children, because genes help shape a body.
items.why: A strong answer picks Grace and is fair to Deepa's idea.

items.p: Draw two bean plants that grew from the same packet of seeds. One sat in the sun and one sat in a dark corner. Show how each plant looks after two weeks.
items.a: One tall green plant in the sun, and one short pale or thin plant in the dark corner.
items.why: The two plants have the same kind of genes, but they grew differently because of the light. Genes and life work together.

items.p: Only children can learn a new language. Grown-ups cannot.
items.why: False. Grown-ups can learn new languages too. It is often easier when you are young, but it can be done at any age.

items.p: Which one is NOT learned?
items.why: Eye colour comes from genes. Speaking Marathi, swimming and writing are learned.

items.p: Thenu, a girl in Class 2, has two tall parents. She eats good food and sleeps well. Why is Thenu tall?
opts: Because of her genes and her food
items.why: Height comes from genes and from good food and health, so it is a bit of both.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down. Scientists dropped a touch-me-not plant gently, again and again. At first the plant folded the leaves. Later the plant kept the leaves open. Was this behaviour inherited, or learned? Why do you think so?
items.a: Learned. The plant changed during their own life, after many harmless drops.
items.why: A strong answer says the change came after many drops in the plant's own life. So this was learned, not inherited.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down. A teacher tells a left-handed child to write with the right hand. Is this a good idea? Why do you think so?
items.a: No. Being left-handed is not a bad habit. It starts before birth, and forcing a child to switch hands makes writing harder.
items.why: A strong answer says left-handedness is not a habit that can be trained out.

videos.title: A young zebra finch learns its song from its father
videos.channel: Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST)
videos.why: Shows a young bird learning his song by listening to an older male, so the child sees that other animals learn too.
videos.check: Found by search: "Development of the Juvenile Zebra Finch Song Using the Memory of the Father’s Song" by Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST), 1 minute. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: Tuning in to speech sounds
videos.why: Shows that babies are born able to hear the sounds of every language, and tune in to the language around them.
videos.check: Found by search: "Tuning In to Speech Sounds" by Reading Rockets, 3 minutes. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: Mother chimpanzee teaches her baby to catch termites
videos.why: Shows a young chimpanzee watching her mother and copying her, so the child sees a skill passed on by watching.
videos.check: Found by search: "Mother Chimpanzee Teaches Baby to Catch Termites | Natural World: Wild Mother and Babies | BBC Earth" by BBC Earth, 4 minutes. A parent may preview it.

quiz.p: Revathi, a girl in Class 2, has her Amma's curly hair. How did she get it?
opts: She inherited it from her parents
quiz.why: Curly hair comes from genes that Revathi got from her parents.

quiz.p: A girl has long fingers like her grandmother, draws kolam like her grandmother, and speaks Tamil like her grandmother. Which one did she get from her grandmother when she was born?
quiz.why: Long fingers come through genes. Kolam and Tamil words are learned from the people around her.

quiz.p: Joseph, a boy in Kottayam, can swim across the pond. How did he get this skill?
opts: He got it from his Appa's genes
quiz.why: Swimming is a skill. Joseph learned it by practising.

quiz.p: In the Practice Test, why do we throw from the same line in every round?
quiz.why: If the line moved closer, more balls would go in, even without practice. Keeping it the same makes the test fair.

quiz.p: Anjali, a girl in Class 2, has a new baby brother. Anjali's Amma speaks five languages. What will the baby speak on the day he is born?
opts: No language yet. He will learn from the people around him
quiz.why: Languages are learned. A baby is born able to learn any language, but speaks none on the first day.

quiz.p: In the 1880s, August Weismann cut the tails off mice. What tails did their babies have?
quiz.why: The babies all had full tails. A change made to a parent's body is not passed on at birth.

quiz.p: Which one comes from both genes and life?
quiz.why: Height comes from genes and from food and health. Eye colour comes from genes. Speaking Odia is learned.

quiz.p: A young male zebra finch grows up alone and never hears another finch sing. What happens to his song?
opts: It is a normal finch song
It comes out strange and broken
quiz.why: A young zebra finch learns his song from an older male. Without one to listen to, his song comes out strange.

quiz.p: Why do young chimpanzees watch their mothers fish for termites with a stick?
opts: They learn how to do it by watching
quiz.why: Young chimpanzees learn to fish for termites by watching their mothers, and then trying.

quiz.p: Shabnam, a girl in Class 2, comes from a family that has drawn rangoli for many generations. Shabnam is very good at it. What is the best reason?
opts: She practised with her family for years
quiz.why: Rangoli is a skill. It passes from person to person by teaching and practice, not through genes.

applications: Teachers and coaches plan practice step by step, because skills are learned and grow with practice.
Doctors ask about a child's parents and grandparents, because some illnesses come through genes and run in families.
Plant breeders choose parent plants with the features they want. Janaki Ammal, a plant scientist from Kerala, crossed sugarcane plants at Coimbatore to make sweet canes that grow well in India.
Language classes and schools help children and grown-ups learn new languages at any age.

spotted.text: A kolam or rangoli at a doorway in the morning, drawn by someone who practised for years.
spotted.art: A white rice-flour kolam at the doorstep of a flat, with a pair of chappals beside it.

spotted.text: A mother cat with her kittens, the kittens copying her as she stalks and pounces.
spotted.art: A tabby mother cat crouching on a wall, with two kittens behind her copying her crouch.

spotted.text: Children learning to ride cycles in a building compound, with someone running behind.
spotted.art: A small girl on a cycle in a building compound, her older sister running behind holding the seat.

spotted.text: A family that speaks two or three languages at home, like Tamil and Telugu, or Bengali and Hindi.
spotted.art: A family at a dining table, the grandmother talking to a child, speech bubbles in two different scripts.

open_questions.q: How much of being good at music or sport comes from genes, and how much from practice?
open_questions.why_open: Studies of twins show both matter. Scientists are still working out how the two work together for each skill.

open_questions.q: Can a parent's life leave small marks that pass to a child?
open_questions.why_open: Genes can be switched on and off. Some scientists think things like hunger in a parent may change these switches in a child. Others say the evidence is weak. It is still argued about.

open_questions.q: Why do young children usually learn a new language more easily than grown-ups?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists agree it is often easier when young. They argue about why, and about whether there is a best age to start.

ask_kids: Who taught you that? Was it a parent, a friend or a teacher?
What is one thing you can do now that you could not do last month?
What did you get from your parents that you did not have to learn?
Look at the crow at the window. Do you think she learned anything today?
If you could learn any skill from anyone in your family, which would it be?

jokes.j: Why did the cycle fall over?
What did the baby say when someone asked if he could talk?
Why did the zebra finch go to music class?
jokes.a: To learn to tweet in tune.

jokes.j: Why did the girl bring a ladder to her singing lesson?
What did the genes say to the skills?
jokes.a: We gave you your eyes. Now you have to learn the rest!

jokes.j: Why was the dosa so good at flipping?
jokes.a: It practised every morning on the tawa.

jokes.j: Why did the kolam never get lost?
jokes.a: It always looped round and came back home.

jokes.j: What do you call a dog who learned magic tricks?

maths.problem: Nandini did the Practice Test three times. Round 1: 3 balls went in. Round 2: 6 went in. Round 3: 7 went in. Between which two rounds did she improve the most?
maths.explain: From Round 1 to Round 2, she went from 3 to 6. That is 3 more. From Round 2 to Round 3, she went from 6 to 7. That is 1 more. 3 is bigger than 1, so she improved most between Round 1 and Round 2.
maths.context: This is about the Practice Test, where you threw paper balls into a bucket before and after practice.
maths.why_maths: Finding the differences between rounds shows when practice helped the most.

maths.problem: Selvi asked 8 relatives who taught them their best skill. A parent: 4 people. A teacher: 2 people. A friend: 1 person. A brother or sister: 1 person. Draw a pictograph with one face for each person. Who taught the most people?
maths.explain: Draw a row for each kind of teacher. A parent gets 4 faces, a teacher 2, a friend 1 and a brother or sister 1. The parent row is the longest. 4 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 8, so every person is shown.
maths.context: This is about the family survey, where you found out who taught each skill.
maths.why_maths: A pictograph shows at a glance who taught the most people.

maths.problem: Revathi counted the breaks in her kolam line each day for a week: 6, 5, 5, 3, 2, 2, 1. How many fewer breaks did she make on day 7 than on day 1? On how many days was the number the same as the day before?
maths.answer: 5 fewer breaks. On 2 days the number was the same as the day before.
maths.explain: 6 take away 1 leaves 5. Day 3 had 5, the same as day 2. Day 6 had 2, the same as day 5. So the number stayed the same on 2 days, and still went down over the week.
maths.context: This is about the Seven-Day Kolam, where you drew the same kolam every day and counted the breaks.
maths.why_maths: Counting the breaks each day turns a skill growing into numbers you can compare.

warmup.a: To get a feature from your parents, through their genes.
Riding a cycle, swimming, speaking a language or drawing a kolam.

warmup.q: Can practice make your thumb longer?
warmup.a: No. The length of your thumb comes from genes.

warmup.q: Is a baby born speaking a language?
warmup.a: No. A baby learns the language spoken around them.

warmup.q: Is height from genes, from food, or both?
warmup.a: Both. Genes and good food and health.

warmup.q: How does a young zebra finch learn his song?
warmup.a: By listening to an older male finch.

founder: ideas/by_topic/genes-and-inheriting-features.md: the science journal pages on a family tree with traits (p2 to p3) became the family survey, which adds a column for skills and who taught them. The SCI card on Janaki Ammal became an application. The notebook's RNA story and most cards are for older levels.

Cambridge Primary Science Stage 2, 4.3 Inheriting characteristics: animals inherit characteristics from both parents and look similar but not identical. This unit adds the other half of the covers line: what we learn.
science: Weismann, A. (1889). Essays upon Heredity. He removed the tails of mice for five generations; all offspring had normal tails.
Lamarck, J.-B. (1809). Philosophie zoologique: inheritance of characters acquired by use and disuse.

Werker, J. F. and Tees, R. C. (1984). Cross-language speech perception: evidence for perceptual reorganization during the first year of life. Infant Behavior and Development 7: 49 to 63. English-learning infants discriminated the Hindi dental and retroflex stops at 6 to 8 months, and few did at 10 to 12 months.
Maguire, E. A. and others (2000). Navigation-related structural change in the hippocampi of taxi drivers. PNAS 97: 4398 to 4403. Posterior hippocampus larger in London taxi drivers.
Lonsdorf, E. V., Eberly, L. E. and Pusey, A. E. (2004). Sex differences in learning in chimpanzees. Nature 428: 715 to 716. Daughters watched mothers termite-fish more and learned earlier than sons.

Gagliano, M. and others (2014). Experience teaches plants to learn faster and forget slower in environments where it matters. Oecologia 175: 63 to 72. Mimosa pudica stopped folding after repeated harmless drops and kept this for weeks, while still folding to shaking.
Zebra finch song learning from an adult male tutor; isolated males develop abnormal song (for example Immelmann 1969; Price 1979).
Handedness: about 10 percent of people are left-handed; partly heritable, and identical twins are often discordant (McManus and others).
Height: highly heritable, and average heights rose in many countries over the twentieth century with better nutrition and health (NCD Risk Factor Collaboration, eLife 2016).
Newborn grasp reflex: present from birth.
Janaki Ammal worked at the Sugarcane Breeding Station in Coimbatore in the 1930s and produced hybrid sugarcane suited to Indian conditions.
Thirukkural 396. Bhagavad Gita 6.35. Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book II, chapter 1.

roots.context: We have tested what practice can change and what it cannot. Now we ask what this tells us about who we are.

deep_truth.truth: In your test, practice made your throws land better, but your thumb stayed the same length. Your thumb's length comes mostly from the genes you got from your parents. Your throwing skill grew from your own tries. A skill is not passed on at birth, so every child must learn it again.
deep_truth.habit: We say a skill 'runs in the family', as if it came with the body. The test shows that features come through genes, while skills come through practice and teaching.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Practice Test, more balls went in the bucket after five minutes of practice. The thumb mark on the paper strip stayed in the same place.

three.who_am_i: You are made of what you got from your family, and of everything you have practised.
three.what_is_life: Living beings get their bodies from their parents, and keep learning all their lives. A finch, a touch-me-not plant and you all learn.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of skills that pass from one being to another by teaching: songs, kolams, recipes and languages.

roots.thread: Every child starts with features from a long line of parents. Then each child adds skills of their own, learned from the people and the world around them. Skills pass by teaching, so a skill can go to anyone who learns it, not only to a child of the family. In this way, one big family of life keeps sharing what each member learns.

teachings.teaching: The deeper you dig a well in the sand, the more water flows. The more a person learns, the more their understanding flows.
teachings.link: Your throws got better with every try. Learning builds up a little at a time, the way a well gets deeper with each dig.

teachings.teaching: Krishna tells Arjuna that the restless mind is hard to steady. But it can be steadied by practice and by letting go.
teachings.link: Practice does not only change a hand or an aim. Even the mind can be changed by practice.

teachings.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book II, chapter 1
teachings.teaching: We become builders by building, and lyre players by playing the lyre, a small harp.
teachings.link: Nobody is born a good thrower or a kolam artist. We become one by doing it again and again.

science.text: Skills a parent learns are not passed on to children through genes. Each child learns them again.
Scientists are studying whether a parent's life, such as going hungry, can change which genes are switched on in a child.

other_view.view: Twin studies show that genes also shape how easily a person learns some skills, like music or running. So for them, being good at something is never only practice. Genes and practice work together.

practice.title: Born Breath, Learned Breath
practice.say: Sit still, with your hands in your lap. Just breathe, the way you always do. Nobody taught you to breathe. You could do it the moment you were born. Now let us try a learned breath. Breathe in slowly while I count to four. Breathe out slowly while I count to four. Do it three more times. Was the last one easier than the first? That is practice, working on you right now.
practice.kid: Sit still. Just breathe. You were born knowing how. Now breathe in to four. Breathe out to four. Do it four times. Did it get easier?

ask: If you could choose, would you rather be born with a skill, or learn it yourself? Why?
When an older person teaches you a kolam, do they still have it? Who has it now?
A touch-me-not plant learns, a finch learns, and you learn. Is learning the same thing in all three?
roots.art: A girl sitting cross-legged on a balcony with her eyes closed, breathing slowly, with a kolam on the floor in front of her and a potted touch-me-not beside her.

how_we_found_out.context: People once thought that what parents did to their own bodies was passed on to their babies. This card tells the true story of how that idea was tested.
how_we_found_out.story: For a very long time, many people thought that changes in a parent's life were passed on to their babies at birth. A blacksmith with strong arms would have babies with strong arms. In 1809, the French scientist Jean-Baptiste Lamarck wrote about an idea like this. He thought a giraffe who stretched up for leaves passed a slightly longer neck to her young. In the late 1880s, the German scientist August Weismann tested the idea. He cut off the tails of young mice. When they grew up and had babies, he cut those babies' tails too. He did this for five generations of mice. Hundreds of babies were born, and every one had a full tail. A change made to a parent's body was not passed on. It was not a perfect test, because a cut tail is an injury, not a body part the mouse used more. But many later tests found the same thing. Today, scientists still argue about whether a parent's life can leave small marks on a child, through switches on the genes.
how_we_found_out.who: Jean-Baptiste Lamarck, a French scientist (1809); August Weismann, a German scientist (late 1880s)
how_we_found_out.when: Lamarck wrote his idea in 1809. Weismann did his mouse test in the late 1880s and wrote about it in 1889.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That changes a parent makes to their own body during life are passed on to their babies at birth. Weismann's mice had their tails cut for five generations, and every baby was still born with a full tail.
how_we_found_out.art: A bearded scientist in an old laboratory looking at a cage of white mice, every mouse with a full tail.

playtest: Walked through the unit as a parent and child in a flat. The Practice Test needs only paper balls, a bucket and a paper strip; the thumb measure now starts with the strip level with the thumb tip, and a pencil-width difference is explained as measuring, not growing. Both games are written out card by card; the sorting game now has points so it ends with a winner, and the memory game's cards each name who they are about, so no card matches two others. Removed repeated questions (the thumb result, kolam breaks, mouse tails), a weak joke and assumed family members, and made the survey table match its questions.
